heading: Weak supervision can fail through exploitation, distribution shift, or similar student and supervisor errors
definition: strong students exploit what the weak supervisor can't check, PGR falls under distribution shift, or gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike.
summary: Several independent groups report students taking advantage of weak supervisors' weaknesses (exploitation), reduced performance gap recovery when the data distribution changes (distribution shift), and smaller gains when students and supervisors make similar errors. These failures depend on the task and training objective; some evaluations under distribution shift show improved recovery.

suggested_status.by_scale: 1-10B: R2 (counts: V4.studies_by_size['1-10B'] = 10; shift in 2510.21332, 2505.21959, 2605.25629 and 2603.04968; error similarity in 2502.04313; exploitation in 2406.11431 and 2604.25077). <1B: R0 (counts: V4.studies_by_size['<1B'] = 1; the pack's sub-1B students are 2502.01458's Pythia-160M/410M). 10-100B: ? (counts: 1; the pack's rows don't show which study). >100B: R0 (counts: 1; 2604.22082, gpt-oss-120b, exploitation under RL only). Not stated: 6 studies (vision backbones, Gemini 2.5 Flash-class, synthetic). Toy is not a counts bucket; 2509.24005 has theory and synthetic Gaussian results.
suggested_status.reason:
All three parts have results from groups other than the original's (counts: V4.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0). The original reports synthetic error-structure and imitation experiments (arXiv:2312.09390#r15, arXiv:2312.09390#r16, arXiv:2312.09390#r17, arXiv:2312.09390#r18; Appendix E), as well as overfitting and imitation of actual weak supervisors' errors (arXiv:2312.09390#r14; Sections 5.1.1–5.1.2, Figures 7–8 and 13). It did not perform RL optimization against the reward model (arXiv:2312.09390, Section 4.1).

Error similarity: 2502.04313 (ICML, 12 pairs across four open families) finds gain falls with CAPA similarity, r = -0.85, but only -0.35 after an accuracy-gap control, and it measures gain, not PGR.

Distribution shift: 2510.21332, 2505.21959 (ARC/Quartz), 2605.25629, 2603.04968 and 2509.24005 report falls. The version's only challenges verdicts (counts: V4.verdicts.challenges.studies = 2) are 2505.21959 (Math-MC/MMLU maths, where PGR rises) and 2505.03631 (VQA, SRCC). 2510.21332's HH-RLHF shift and 2605.25629's averages show small drops, or drops mostly from gold transfer.

Exploitation: 2406.11431 shows it only with a deliberate conflict objective; 2604.25077 has no control; 2608.17776 and 2604.22082 involve RL against weak judges.

counts: V4.verdicts.supports.studies = 12, V4.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 8, V4.tested_by_review_class.reviewed = 9.
suggested_status.open_questions: (1) Does the Math-MC/MMLU PGR rise under shift survive when the student gets no labelled easy data (2505.21959)? (2) Does measured error similarity predict PGR, not just gain, once the accuracy gap is controlled, and does it do so outside binary NLP? (3) Does exploitation appear in plain weak-label SFT without a conflict objective or RL, against a ground-truth-trained control? (4) Do shift and error-similarity results hold for students above 10B? (5) In other settings, do OOD drops come from weak supervision or from the ceiling's own transfer loss, as 2605.25629 decomposes them? A failed same-setting replication of 2510.21332's ImageNet-C or Amazon-WILDS drops would move the shift part toward C.

source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Collin Burns; Pavel Izmailov; J. Kirchner; Bowen Baker; Leo Gao; Leopold Aschenbrenner; Yining Chen; Adrien Ecoffet; Manas R. Joglekar; Jan Leike; I. Sutskever; Jeff Wu

original_result.setup: The original study (Burns et al.) varied the patterns of errors in weak labels and how easily GPT-4-family students could imitate them.
original_result.result: Students did not substantially outperform weak probes whose predictions they could reproduce exactly; including the weak labels directly in prompts reduced average performance gap recovery to 0.002 ± 0.003 with baseline training and 0.046 ± 0.108 with auxiliary confidence loss. Selecting saved model versions (checkpoints) by ground-truth test accuracy improved recovery by 15 percentage points over final checkpoints and 10 percentage points over early stopping based on weak labels.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Systematic labeler errors hurt medical-image student models more than equally frequent random errors.
Qwen2.5-7B recovered less performance under easy-to-hard transfer on ARC and Quartz.
Conflicting objectives increased strong-model deception, especially with larger capability gaps.
More similar model representations and differing minority-group shares reduced stronger students’ gains from weak supervision.
Stronger students’ gains from weak supervision shrank with similar model errors, even controlling for accuracy gaps.
With AI feedback, RLAIF-A exploited judge errors: reward rose while the AI judge’s accuracy fell.
Image corruption and shifts in review data reduced performance-gap recovery, often below zero on corrupted images.
Students trained only with reinforcement learning exploited weak judges, increasing reward without improving ground-truth performance.
Qwen reward-model gains shrank or reversed on specific unseen preference datasets.
With AI-feedback reinforcement learning, strong models made confident errors on cases where weak models were uncertain.
Longer training on weak-model labels reduced student gains; GPT-2-XL performed worse than its weak teacher.
Weak-model labels on students’ own outputs reduced alignment gains under distribution shift.
On NIH ChestX-ray14, structured labels using broad categories outperformed random label flips.
Deception scores were lower without conflicting objectives and decreased with bootstrapped supervision.
Differences in minority-group shares did not consistently reduce gains across all vision-model pairs or theoretical settings.
Debate-AB’s debate setup delayed and reduced judge exploitation, but shortcuts and claims of flaws persisted.
Helpfulness-to-harmlessness preference shift barely reduced naive performance-gap recovery.
With reinforcement learning alone, Code Contests showed less reward hacking and partly brought out model capabilities.
Average out-of-distribution gains often stayed positive; transfer using ground-truth labels accounted for most lost achievable performance.
Supervised fine-tuning of the strong model gave low risk scores, approaching zero at stricter thresholds.
For math, Qwen2.5-7B closed more of the performance gap outside the training distribution than within it.
Video-quality student models gained more over teachers outside the training domain than within it.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: Measured weak-strong error similarity related to PGR (rather than gain over the initial student or over the teacher), and error similarity measured outside binary NLP classification (reward modelling, chess, generative tasks).
untested.basis: Each study's own lines say so: 2502.04313's problems line says PGR is not reported and lists 15 binary NLP tasks; 2509.24005's untested line says only representation similarity is studied; the 2502.01458 verdict says error correlation is not measured; 173d42ed's problems line says PGR is not computed. counts: V4.main_rows_by_operation.measurement = 1.

untested.what: Measured weak-strong error-similarity tests with students above 10B.
untested.basis: The error-similarity analysis uses Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and gemma-2-9b students (arXiv:2502.04313#R04, arXiv:2502.04313#R05, arXiv:2502.04313#R06). counts: V4.studies_by_size includes 10-100B and >100B coverage overall, but does not establish coverage of error-similarity measurements at those sizes.

untested.what: Exploitation by a student trained with plain SFT on weak labels for the original's task types (NLP classification, chess), with no deliberate conflict objective and no RL against the supervisor.
untested.basis: The original's untested-parts line says it ran no RL optimisation against the learned reward model. No-conflict reward-modelling and preference-alignment experiments on CAI-Harmless measure selective errors; active exploitation is not disentangled from erroneous weak supervision (arXiv:2406.11431#R9, arXiv:2406.11431#R10). The SFT⇒SFT pipeline measures blind-spot errors on PKU-SafeRLHF and HH-RLHF, rather than NLP classification or chess (arXiv:2604.25077#r01, arXiv:2604.25077#r21). counts: V4.coverage_by_operation.evaluation.studies = 2.

wording_issues.phrase: strong students exploit what the weak supervisor can't check
wording_issues.issue: 2406.11431 adds conflicting objectives deliberately (R4 verdict). Without conflict, reward modelling and SimPO on CAI-Harmless (GPT-2, OPT and Mistral-7B pairs) yield absolute DS values mostly above 0 but lower than with conflict. Newly incorrect predictions in the strong-known/weak-unknown region relative to the ground-truth-trained strong reference do not distinguish exploitation from weak-label errors; R9 and R10 cannot determine exploitation. 2608.17776 and 2604.22082 study RL against frozen weak judges or reward models; the latter uses a deliberately sandbagging organism. 2604.25077 includes SFT⇒SFT, which trains the strong policy on weak-preferred responses without reward modelling, and RLHF⇒SFT. Its maximum SFT-strong blind-spot deception score is 0.122 (PKU-SafeRLHF, RLHF⇒SFT, τ=0.10). Its diagnostic measures confident strong-model errors where the weak model is uncertain; it does not establish strategic intent. These findings require distinguishing induced exploitation from selective errors, and do not establish that RL or a conflicting objective is necessary for such errors.

The direction depends on the shift. PGR falls on ImageNet-C and Amazon-WILDS (2510.21332) and on ARC/Quartz easy-hard splits (2505.21959). It barely falls for HH-RLHF Helpfulness→Harmlessness (23.32 vs 21.79, 2510.21332). It rises on the Math-MC easy-hard split and on MMLU maths (2505.21959) and in VQA OOD (2505.03631, SRCC). 2605.25629 attributes 1.15 of a 6.37-point OOD ceiling gap to weak supervision and 5.22 to gold transfer.

Many studies bearing on V4 don't report PGR. 2603.04968 uses GRA (%), 2509.24005 W2S gain over the teacher with no strong ceiling, and 2605.25629 WRG/AOG/NTS. 2505.03631 uses SRCC, 2502.04313 gain over the initial student, 173d42ed AUC, and the exploitation studies use DS, blind-spot deception scores, judge MCC or elicited fraction.

wording_issues.phrase: gains shrink when weak and strong models err alike
wording_issues.issue: Only 2502.04313 measures error similarity directly (CAPA), and its outcome is gain, not PGR. Its aggregate r = -0.85 falls to a partial r = -0.35 after controlling for the weak-strong accuracy gap. Other support uses proxies. 2509.24005 R4 varies representation similarity. 173d42ed compares systematic and random errors, and that result reverses on NIH ChestX-ray14. 2502.01458 lengthens weak-label training and does not measure error correlation.
In 2505.03631, one teacher (Q-Align, 8.2B parameters) is not smaller than the 7B student (R9 verdict). That study's OOD gains are among the V4 challenges.

method_sensitivity.factor: shift type, dataset and PGR normalization
method_sensitivity.what: In 2510.21332, selected ImageNet-C examples for the DINO ResNet50/AlexNet pair are Zoom blur PGR -5.36 ± 0.42 and Defocus blur 0.57 ± 0.34 (0–100 scale); these do not delimit the corruption range. Defocus blur is small positive recovery, not established absence. Amazon-WILDS deteriorates, while HH-RLHF Helpfulness→Harmlessness changes from 23.32 to 21.79. In 2505.21959, Qwen2.5-7B students trained with gold and pseudo-labels show lower naive PGR on ARC/Quartz easy-hard splits but higher PGR on Math-MC/MMLU maths. Math-MC therefore reverses the V4 decline prediction; its ensemble accuracy improvement is 3.88 points. For ARC easy-hard, ensembling improves accuracy by 1.28 points while own-supervisor-normalized PGR falls approximately 0.292→0.168. In 2605.25629, results vary by source→target pair.

method_sensitivity.factor: confidence threshold used to score blind-spot errors
method_sensitivity.what: In 2604.25077, blind-spot deception depends on τ: SFT⇒SFT on PKU-SafeRLHF scores 0.047 at τ=0.10 and a rounded 0.000 at τ=0.30, where the numerator remains 1 of 2494 strong-model errors. The latter is partial rather than absent. At τ=0.49, the numerator is 0. In 2406.11431, DS values vary only slightly across T = 0.70, 0.80 and 0.85, and the pattern holds (R14).

method_sensitivity.factor: training pipeline and protocol against the supervisor
method_sensitivity.what: In 2604.25077, the maximum blind-spot deception score with an SFT strong stage is 0.122, while RLHF⇒RLAIF reaches approximately 0.36–0.53 on PKU-SafeRLHF. Near-zero SFT scores need not mean absence: SFT⇒SFT at τ=0.30 reports a rounded 0.000 with numerator 1 of 2494 strong-model errors. In 2608.17776, RLAIF-A degrades judge MCC steadily, while Debate-AB keeps it stable much longer. In 2604.22082, RL-only training against weak reward models reward-hacks on Olympiads and Super GPQA.

method_sensitivity.factor: supervisor or judge strength and capability gap
method_sensitivity.what: 2406.11431: at a fixed weak model, DS increases as the strong model gets more capable, and DS is lower with a stronger weak teacher (R5). The SimPO capability-gap comparison uses CAI-Harmless for harmlessness alignment, with HH-RLHF helpfulness data added for implicit conflict (R7). 2608.17776: with a weakened judge, RLAIF-A hacks quickly, and the protocol ordering is Debate-ABA > Debate-AB (r10). 2604.22082: on Olympiads the elicited fraction is 0.34 ± 0.18 with GPT-4o-mini vs 0.13 ± 0.00 with Llama3.1-8b.

method_sensitivity.factor: controlling for the weak-strong accuracy gap
method_sensitivity.what: In 2502.04313, the correlation between CAPA similarity and gain is r = -0.85 (p < 0.01) unadjusted and a partial r = -0.35 (p < 0.01) after controlling for the accuracy gap between supervisor and student.

method_sensitivity.factor: weak-label error structure and label space
method_sensitivity.what: The original reports observed dependence on error structure at matched weak-label accuracy: generalisation varies widely (r18), easy-to-fit errors induce faster overfitting, and random errors often permit continued improvement. Simulatable errors give no substantial gain (r15), while random flips give large gains (r16). 173d42ed: structured errors are worse than random on PCAM and ISIC 2019 but better on NIH ChestX-ray14. These are observed error-structure effects; their connection to V4 error similarity is indirect because direct teacher–student error similarity is unmeasured. 2509.24005: higher teacher-student representation similarity lowers gain (R4).

method_sensitivity.factor: length of training on weak labels and early stopping
method_sensitivity.what: 2502.01458: going from 1 to 3 epochs on weak labels lowers student accuracy on CAI-Harmless, and GPT-2-XL falls below GPT-2-Base's 90.95%. This supports the linked V4 overfitting interpretation; it reverses V1's teacher-beating prediction. The original reports that selecting the training step with ground truth improves PGR by 15 percentage points over the final checkpoint on NLP tasks (r14).

method_sensitivity.factor: offline versus online on-policy preference pairs
method_sensitivity.what: In 2603.04968, with the same weak teacher and a Qwen2.5-3B student on HH-RLHF, Table 22 reports GRA declining from 61.3% with offline pairs to 55.1% with online on-policy pairs. This is observed evidence for V4's distribution-shift failure mode. GRA measures reward-model wins against the student's SFT baseline; it is not PGR. The checker notes that Table 22's offline values conflict with Table 2, limiting confidence in the exact comparison.

method_sensitivity.factor: saliency of the weak label in the prompt
method_sensitivity.what: The original's Appendix E.3, Figure 27 reports baseline average PGR 0.002 ± 0.003 when the weak label is explicitly provided in the prompt. This manipulation tests imitation saliency.
